title: Gyroscopes: Why Spinning Things Stay Upright
hook: A spinning top won't fall over and a rolling coin stays balanced. Spin gives an object a stubborn sense of direction — angular momentum resists any attempt to tip its axis.
key_points: A spinning object has angular momentum, which resists changes to its spin axis.
That's why a top stays upright and a thrown football spirals true.
Push on a spinning gyroscope and it veers sideways (precession) instead of toppling.
Gyroscopes keep planes, ships, and phones oriented by holding their axis steady.
content_html: Set a top spinning and it stands on its point, defying the fall you'd expect from anything balanced so precariously. The secret is angular momentum: a spinning object resists changes not just to how fast it spins, but to the direction its axis points. The faster it spins, the more stubbornly it holds that direction. The same effect steadies a rolling coin, a thrown football's spiral, and the wheels of a moving bicycle (though a bike's balance also owes a lot to its steering geometry).
extra_html: Things get delightfully counterintuitive when you push on a spinning gyroscope. Instead of toppling the way the push points, its axis swings off at a right angle, slowly circling — an effect called precession. It's the reason a leaning top traces lazy circles rather than crashing down. Engineers put this stubbornness to work: a gyroscope's axis stays fixed in space, providing a reference that lets aircraft, ships, spacecraft, and the tiny sensors in your phone detect exactly how they've turned. Wikipedia explains the angular-momentum mechanics and the many devices built on it.

related.title: Angular Momentum: Why a Skater Speeds Up
related.hook: A spinning figure skater pulls her arms in and whirls faster — without pushing off anything. That's angular momentum being conserved.

related.title: Torque: The Twist That Makes Things Turn
related.hook: Why is a long wrench easier than a short one? Torque is rotational force — it grows with how far from the pivot you push, not just how hard.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a fast-spinning top resist falling over?
flashcards.back_html: Its spin gives it angular momentum, which resists any change to the direction of its axis — so the axis holds steady instead of tipping.

flashcards.prompt: What does a spinning gyroscope do when you push sideways on its axis?

choices.text: Its axis slowly swings at right angles to the push (precession)
It immediately topples in the direction of the push

flashcards.explanation_html: Angular momentum makes a gyroscope respond to a twist at 90° to where you'd expect — the axis precesses rather than falling, which is why tops circle.

flashcards.prompt: How do gyroscopes help navigate planes, ships, and phones?

choices.text: A spinning element holds its orientation, giving a stable reference direction
They generate electricity to power the navigation screen
They attract the device toward magnetic north

flashcards.explanation_html: Because its axis resists turning, a gyroscope provides a fixed reference, letting instruments sense how the vehicle has rotated.
